newsitem.title: CONGO: Congo's shaky truce enters second week.
newsitem.headline: Congo's shaky truce enters second week.

text.p: Brazzaville's shaky truce entered its second week on Wednesday as efforts continued to shore up the ceasefire and put together a pan-African intervention force.

The United Nations has told Congolese President Pascal Lissouba and rival Denis Sassou Nguesso, a former military leader, that they must earn the force by showing the will to find a political reconciliation.
"It's on this point that things are jammed, it is very difficult," French ambassador Raymond Cesaire, the only foreign envoy left in Brazzaville, told Reuters on Wednesday.
"It needs time. Let's cross our fingers."
He said more progress had been made on shoring up the ceasefire and on trying to make the airport, a key target for the warring rivals, safe enough for an intervention force to be able to land.

Togo and Senegal have offered troops for the mission of an expected 1,700 soldiers. Veteran Togolese President Gnassingbe Eyadema has been sounding out West African Francophone states about sending troops.
Cesaire, protected by 30 gendarmes, has been shuttling between Lissouba, Sassou and city mayor Bernard Kolelas, who heads the National Mediation Committee to try and keep the truce going.
The situation on Wednesday morning was the calmest in days.
An estimated 1,000 to 3,000 people, most of them civilians, died in 12 days of fighting that began on June 5 when Lissouba tried to disarm Sassou's private militia, known as the Cobras.

Kolelas, with Cesaire's support, brokered a ceasefire that took hold a week ago. Within three days, the 1,250 French soldiers who had evacuated several thousand foreigners from Brazzaville flew out themselves.
The truce has so far prevented all-out battles but no day has passed without at least sporadic shelling and gunfire -- and people are still dying, albeit in far smaller numbers.
France's 12 diplomats and gendarmes are among a handful of foreigners left in Brazzaville that also includes some missionaries and international Red Cross workers.

Many of the city's diplomats and expatriate businessfolk have decamped to Pointe Noire, Congo's Atlantic Ocean port which, like the rest of the oil-producing country, has been untouched by the fighting in the capital.
Mediation efforts are aimed at getting presidential elections, due on July 27 but postponed due to the fighting, back on track.
Lissouba is trying to get a constitutional council to extend his term of office until October because of the chaos. Sassou says Lissouba is no longer fit to rule and must step down now.
